key_insight: A prescribed-kinematics Resistive Immersed Surface (RIS) model can approximate key aortic-valve hemodynamics from a fully coupled Immersed Boundary (IB) simulation, while being much cheaper to run.
engineering_relevance: This suggests RIS is a practical option for valve-flow studies when realistic leaflet motion is available and rapid hemodynamic estimation is more important than full FSI fidelity.
method: Compare RIS (prescribed leaflet kinematics + penalty forcing) vs. fully coupled IB (elastic leaflets + two-way FSI).
Test both methods on trileaflet and bicuspid aortic valve configurations.
Assess bulk flow structures and transvalvular pressure gradients in SimVascular/svMultiPhysics and IBAMR workflows.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that RIS predicts mean transvalvular pressure gradient within 15% of IB, improving to within 5% when inlet boundary conditions are matched, with about 60% lower computational cost.
watch_item: RIS depends on representative prescribed leaflet kinematics, so inaccuracies in the imposed motion or inlet conditions can degrade its predictive value.
paper_title: Comparative analysis of resistive immersed surface and immersed boundary methods for aortic valve simulation
